blindSummary:
A customary system of bilateral inter-community peace pacts in one constituent area of this state/province - with its own pact-holders, sanctions and dispute-resolution authority over “crimes and tribal-related offences” - was formally codified by that area's provincial government in February 2026 as a 137-page written code. The country's courts recognise the customary system; academic literature frames it as legal pluralism in which indigenous and formal criminal justice coexist, with police handling customary-law cases. For a visitor whose dispute falls under one of these pacts' jurisdiction, the applicable institution may not be a national court.

No trans-specific customary ruling, exclusion or gender-expression punishment was documented in this state/province. Recognition of indigenous justice systems also appears in the organic law underlying the country's present autonomous unit, reinforcing the framework.

Local risk sits marginally below the country-wide average, at the minimum-deviation threshold. The finding is a structural uncertainty (which court applies to you) without any evidence of a trans-specific adverse outcome. Compared with the autonomous unit, where the same legal-pluralism concern is paired with an active criminal-law drafting process (discretionary religious offences) that raises the stakes materially, the customary system here is a civil dispute-resolution institution with no criminal-law expansion documented for morality offences.
